opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that academics have spent their whole careers being rewarded for doing things that are genuinely hard, things that very few people can do. So there's a natural identity investment there. If you've spent twenty years becoming one of maybe a hundred people in the world who really understands some corner of, say, probabilistic inference, it's very uncomfortable to entertain the idea that a model trained for a few months might match you. And I don't say that to be dismissive. I feel it myself.

But I think there's also a more substantive version of the skepticism. People look at current systems and see that they make silly mistakes, they confabulate, they struggle with long-horizon research that requires taste and persistence over months. And those are real limitations today. The issue is that people tend to take a snapshot of the current capabilities and treat it as a fixed ceiling, rather than looking at the trend. If you'd asked people five years ago whether a model could write a decent literature review or catch a bug in a proof, many would have said that's far off too.

There's also something about how academic work feels from the inside. A lot of what we do feels like it depends on this ineffable sense of what's interesting, what question to ask next. And because we can't articulate how we do it, it feels like it must be uniquely human. But "I can't explain how I do it" isn't strong evidence that it can't be learned. Plenty of things we couldn't articulate, like recognizing faces or playing Go well, turned out to be learnable.

And finally, I think there's a bit of a selection effect. The people who are most convinced their jobs can be automated maybe have already left academia for the labs. So the people who remain, on average, are the ones who find that prospect less plausible, or less pressing.

r001.rationale: The response explains why academics may doubt AI could do their jobs, but does not say this skepticism is common beyond academia.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because I'm an academic myself, and I've watched my own colleagues go through this. And honestly, I had a version of this skepticism too, maybe five or six years ago.

I think there are a few things going on. The first is just that academics, more than almost anyone, have built their identity around being smart. Like, the whole career is a series of filters where you got selected for being better at thinking about hard problems than the people around you. So the idea that a machine could do that is not just an economic threat, it's kind of an existential one. It's much easier to say "well, it can't really do the creative part" than to sit with the possibility that the creative part wasn't as special as you thought.

The second thing is that academics tend to evaluate AI on the thing they personally are best at, and at the current moment, there's usually still something there. If you're a really good mathematician, you can find a problem the model flubs. And then you go, "see, it doesn't really understand." But that's kind of the wrong comparison. The question isn't whether the model beats the best person in the world at their specialty today. It's whether it can do the median grad student's job, or the median postdoc's job, and then whether that bar keeps moving. And it has been moving, really fast. I've seen people make confident claims about what AI would never do that got falsified within eighteen months, and then they just quietly update the goalposts rather than updating their worldview.

There's also a more subtle thing, which is that academics are often not very good at seeing how much of their job is actually routine. When you ask a professor what they do, they'll describe the one brilliant insight they had in 2019. They won't describe the literature reviews, the grant writing, the debugging, the writing of the related-work section, the responding to reviewer two. But that stuff is like eighty percent of the actual hours. And a lot of it is already automatable right now.

And I guess the last thing I'd say is, I actually have some sympathy for the skepticism as a pragmatic stance, even when it's wrong as a prediction. If you're a tenured professor, there's not an obvious action you should take in response to "AI will do your job in ten years." So in some sense the skepticism is load-bearing. It's what lets people keep going. I just think we should be honest that that's what it is, rather than treating it as a considered technical judgment. Because the people who actually work closely with these systems, who spend hours a day with them, are mostly not skeptical anymore. The skepticism correlates really strongly with distance from the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response describes skepticism among academics and says they are especially invested in being smart, but it does not say that this reaction is common beyond academia.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that we have a much richer picture of our own jobs than we do of other people’s jobs. So when someone says, “AI is going to automate this other profession,” you think, “Sure, I can imagine that.” But when they say it about your work, you immediately think of all the things that are hard to specify: choosing the right question, noticing that an assumption is wrong, knowing when a result is interesting.

And that’s a reasonable objection to the claim that a system can do your job just because it can pass an exam in your field. Research isn’t just answering questions that someone else has formulated. A lot of the work is figuring out what questions to ask.

But I think there’s a leap from “these systems haven’t demonstrated all of those abilities” to “they could never have those abilities.” I don’t see a good basis for that second claim. It’s hard to describe how we do those things, but that doesn’t mean there’s something fundamentally inaccessible about them.

There’s also an emotional component. If you’ve spent your life developing a particular kind of expertise, the possibility that it could become cheap is a lot to take in. That doesn’t make the skepticism wrong. But I think we should distinguish evidence about what the systems can do from our attachment to the idea that our own contribution is uniquely human.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general reaction: people readily imagine AI automating other professions but resist the claim when it concerns their own work. This frames the skepticism as extending beyond academics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that we see how the sausage gets made. If you work on these systems, you’re very aware of their limitations, and it’s easy to look at something that fails in ways a human never would and conclude that it’s missing something fundamental.

But there’s also a moving target in what we count as doing our jobs. An academic’s job includes writing, teaching, coming up with ideas, running experiments, and exercising judgment. When AI gets better at one of those things, it’s tempting to say, “Well, that was the mechanical part. The real work is this other thing.” Each individual distinction might be reasonable, but it doesn’t establish that the remaining tasks are out of reach.

I’d want to make the skepticism more concrete: which part of your work do you think it can’t do, and what would change your mind? There could be good reasons to expect a particular task to be difficult. But being able to spot flaws in today’s systems is different from having a strong argument about what future systems won’t be able to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses academics’ skepticism about AI doing their jobs, but does not say this reaction is common beyond academia.
